title: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
hook: how does love begin? the sutras' list of means, and the one they call chief
carry: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
tomorrow: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the king and the meal: in the Narada Bhakti Sutras, knowing about a meal doesn't end your hunger, and love is its own fruit. Did you trade some knowing about for being with? Day one thousand two hundred sixteen.
screen: `THE KING AND THE MEAL.` · `ITS OWN FRUIT.`

segments.voice: How did you come to love the thing you love most? A kind of music, a sport, a craft, a city. Did you study your way into it? Or did someone take you along, an uncle with his records, a friend who dragged you to a game, a grandmother who let you stand at the stove? Yesterday the sutras said love is its own fruit, not something knowledge can produce. That leaves a practical question hanging. Then how does it start? Today the sutras give their answer, a short list of means, and then they name the one that matters most.
screen: `HOW DID YOU COME TO LOVE IT?` → `SOMEONE TOOK YOU ALONG.` → `THE SUTRAS' LIST OF MEANS.`

segments.voice: The teachers sing of its means, the sutras say, and then they list them. Letting go of the pull of sense objects, and of clinging attachment. Worship that doesn't break off. Hearing and singing the qualities of the Lord, even while living an ordinary life in the world. That last phrase matters. The means aren't only for people in a monastery. They happen at work, in the car, in the kitchen. Then the sutras turn. But chiefly, they say, it comes by the grace of great souls, or by a drop of the Lord's own grace. Chiefly. After the list of things a person can do, the main source is something given. Then three words about the company of the great, mahat-sanga. It is hard to find. It is hard to fathom. And it never fails. Hard to find: such people don't advertise. Hard to fathom: from the outside, it isn't easy to tell who they are. Never fails: in the sutras' view, that company always bears fruit. And how is that company found? Even it, the sutras say, comes only by his grace. Then comes a line that holds the whole section together. Between him and his people, there is no difference. To be near those who love God, in this text, is already to be near God. And the section ends with a sentence said twice, like a teacher tapping the table: strive for that alone, strive for that alone. Back to your uncle with his records. In the sutras' picture, love of God can travel the same way. Someone who already has it takes you along.
screen: `LET GO, WORSHIP, HEAR AND SING.` · `CHIEFLY: THE GRACE OF GREAT SOULS.` · `HARD TO FIND, NEVER FAILS.` · `NO DIFFERENCE: HIM AND HIS PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear and sing, inwardly. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a song, a chant or a name that others once sang around you, at a temple, at home, in a car with the radio on. Let it play quietly inside, without moving your lips. Listen to it the way you'd listen in a room full of people singing it together. When the mind wanders, come back to the next line. If you pray, you can let it be a song of praise to God. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. In the sutras it is helped along by letting go, by worship, by hearing and singing, and chiefly by the company of great souls, mahat-sanga.
Your line: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete. Today, spend ten minutes near someone whose love for something is bigger than yours, and just listen. Day one thousand two hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: In devotional Hindu communities, people gather for satsang, sitting with teachers and fellow devotees to hear and sing about God, and the Narada Bhakti Sutras' lines on the company of great souls are a familiar reason given for it.

pairs: hard to find, hard to fathom
by the grace of great souls

myth: the sutras say love's means are only for monks and nuns

after the list of practices: but chiefly, by the grace of great souls, or a drop of the Lord's grace.

hard to find, hard to fathom, and it never fails.

fork.setup: you've been told love is its own fruit. you want it anyway. what do the sutras name as the chief way it comes?
options: the grace of great souls, or a drop of the Lord's grace.
fork.reveal: they list letting go, unbroken worship, and hearing and singing, then say chiefly it comes by the grace of great souls, or a drop of the Lord's grace.

original.note: Sanskrit mahat-saṅga, the company of the great: the sutras call it hard to find, hard to fathom, and never failing.

trapdoor: what you thought: you get devotion by trying harder.
what it means: the sutras list practices, then say love chiefly comes through the company and grace of those who already love.
what a scholar hears: mahat-saṅgas tu durlabho 'gamyo 'moghaś ca, and then tasmiṃs taj-jane bhedābhāvāt: no difference between the Lord and his people.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

sources.ref: Narada Bhakti Sutras 34–42 (the means: letting go of objects and attachment, unbroken worship, hearing and singing; chiefly the grace of great souls; the company of the great; no difference between him and his people; strive for that alone)

notes: Sutras 34–42 paraphrased. The explanations of 'hard to find, hard to fathom, never fails' are the script's gloss, not the text; confirm they are within the range of the commentaries.
Sutra 41 (tasmiṃs taj-jane bhedābhāvāt) rendered 'between him and his people there is no difference'; confirm.
'Love of God can travel the same way' is framed as the sutras' picture, not a claim about people in general; confirm it reads that way.
howItsDone names satsang; the link to these sutras is given as 'a familiar reason', not a claim about all communities.

Editor pass: the gloss on 'never fails' no longer tells the listener that something in them changes; it is now the sutras' view. Practice rewritten to inward hearing and singing (sutra 37) because remembering a person who passed something on repeated day 1202's practice.
